steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Neural Networks are efficient at approximating any function, and that has made them the default choice in many machine learning tasks. It is the same in deep reinforcement learning (RL), where the introduction of the DQN algorithm started the development of various neural solutions. Earlier neuroscientific explanations said that brainpower resides in combinations coming from trillions of connections, and in line with this present advances have emphasised the role of the neural architecture. So RL improvements have first mostly come from enhancing algorithms and only recently from searching for performing architectural patterns, via automatic deep policy search, or via decoupling object detection and policy search.

But research has also shown more and more that individual neurons shoulder more complexity than was expected at first, and the latest results show that dendritic compartments can compute complex functions (e.g. XOR), which were previously categorised as unsolvable by single-neuron systems. This finding seems to have renewed the interest in activation functions. Many functions have in fact been adopted across different domains. To reduce the bias that a fixed activation function introduces and get higher expressive power, one can also learn which activation function performs well for a particular task, learn to combine arbitrary families of activation functions, or find coefficients for polynomial activations as weights to be optimised.

- Rational activations
  - learn rational activation functions (ratio of polynomials) at each layer
  - converge to any continuous function, better approximants than polynomials
  - adapt while learning -> high neural plasticity [quote: definition of plasticity]
  - suited to dynamic RL; Fig. 1 “Time Pilot”
- This work
  - plasticity important for RL agents; rationals augment it; how many layer weights can be replaced
  - contributions: residual plasticity; joint-rational variant (weight-sharing); DQN and Rainbow on Atari; overestimation reduced
- Structure: plasticity, rationals, empirical evaluation, related work

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Neural Networks are efficient at approximating any function, and that has made them the default choice in many machine learning tasks. It is the same in deep reinforcement learning (RL), where the introduction of the DQN algorithm started the development of various neural solutions. Earlier neuroscientific explanations said that brainpower resides in combinations coming from trillions of connections, and in line with this present advances have emphasised the role of the neural architecture. So RL improvements have first mostly come from enhancing algorithms and only recently from searching for performing architectural patterns, via automatic deep policy search, or via decoupling object detection and policy search.

But research has also shown more and more that individual neurons shoulder more complexity than was expected at first, and the latest results show that dendritic compartments can compute complex functions (e.g. XOR), which were previously categorised as unsolvable by single-neuron systems. This finding seems to have renewed the interest in activation functions. Many functions have in fact been adopted across different domains. To reduce the bias that a fixed activation function introduces and get higher expressive power, one can also learn which activation function performs well for a particular task, learn to combine arbitrary families of activation functions, or find coefficients for polynomial activations as weights to be optimised.

These prior approaches have all contributed to the scenarios they investigated, but there is a finer approach which elegantly encapsulates the challenges that come with reinforcement learning problems. Specifically, we can learn rational activation functions (ratio of polynomials) at each layer. Rationals can converge to any continuous function, and they have also been proven to be better approximants than polynomials in terms of convergence. Even more important, their ability to adapt while learning gives a model high neural plasticity (“capability to adjust to the environment and its transformations”). We argue that adapting to environmental changes is essential, which makes rational activation functions particularly suitable for dynamic RL environments. For a visual intuition, we show an exemplary evolution of two rational activation functions and their changing input distributions in the dynamic “Time Pilot” environment in Fig. 1.

In this work we show that plasticity is of major importance for RL agents, as a central element for satisfying the requirements that come from diverse and dynamic environments, and we propose to use rational activation functions to augment the plasticity of deep RL agents. Besides showing that adaptive activation functions are suitable for Deep RL, we also evaluate how many additional layer weights can be replaced by rational activations. Our specific contributions are:

We motivate why neural plasticity is a key aspect for Deep RL agents and that rational activations are adequate as adaptable activation functions. For this we not only highlight that rational activation functions adapt their parameters over time, but we also prove that they can dynamically embed residual connections, which we call residual plasticity.

Additional representational capacity can hinder generalisation, especially in RL, so we propose a joint-rational variant, which uses weight-sharing in rational activations across different layers.

We show empirically that rational activations bring significant improvements to DQN and Rainbow algorithms on Atari games and that our joint variant increases performance further.

Finally, we investigate the overestimation phenomenon, i.e. predicting too large return values, which has been argued before to come from an unsuitable representational capacity of the learning architecture. Because of the (rational) neural and residual plasticity we introduce, this overestimation can be reduced in practice.

We proceed as follows. First we argue for plasticity in deep RL, then we show how rational functions are particularly suitable candidates to provide plasticity in neural networks and present our empirical evaluation. Before concluding, we touch upon related work.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Neural Networks' efficiency in approximating any function has made them the default choice in many machine learning tasks. Deep reinforcement learning (RL) is no different, as the introduction of the DQN algorithm [1] has sparked the development of various neural solutions. In line with former neuroscientific explanations of brainpower residing in combinations stemming from trillions of connections [2], present advances have emphasised the role of the neural architecture [3,4]. As such, RL improvements have first been obtained mainly through enhancing algorithms [5,6,7] and only recently by searching for performing architectural patterns, via automatic deep policy search [8,9], or via decoupling object detection [10,11] and policy search [12,13].

However, research has also progressively shown that individual neurons shoulder more complexity than initially expected, with the latest results demonstrating that dendritic compartments can compute complex functions (e.g. XOR) [14] previously categorised as unsolvable by single-neuron systems. This finding seems to have renewed interest in activation functions [15,16], and many functions have been adopted across different domains [17,18,19]. To reduce the bias introduced by a fixed activation function and achieve higher expressive power, one can further learn which activation function is performant for a particular task [20,3], learn to combine arbitrary families of activation functions [21], or find coefficients for polynomial activations as weights to be optimised [22].

While these prior approaches have all contributed to their respective scenarios, there exists a finer approach that elegantly encapsulates the challenges brought on by reinforcement learning problems: at each layer, we can learn rational activation functions (ratio of polynomials) [23]. Not only can rationals converge to any continuous function, they have further been proven to be better approximants than polynomials in terms of convergence [24]. More crucially, their ability to adapt while learning equips a model with high neural plasticity (“capability to adjust to the environment and its transformations” [2]). We argue that adapting to environmental changes is essential, which makes rational activation functions particularly suitable for dynamic RL environments. As a visual intuition, we showcase an exemplary evolution of two rational activation functions together with their changing input distributions in the dynamic “Time Pilot” environment in Fig. 1.

In this work, we show that plasticity is of major importance for RL agents, as a central element for satisfying the requirements of diverse and dynamic environments, and propose the use of rational activation functions to augment the plasticity of deep RL agents. Apart from demonstrating the suitability of adaptive activation functions for Deep RL, we also evaluate how many additional layer weights can be replaced by rational activations. Our specific contributions are:

We motivate why neural plasticity is a key aspect for Deep RL agents and why rational activations are adequate as adaptable activation functions. To this end, we not only highlight that rational activation functions adapt their parameters over time, but further prove that they can dynamically embed residual connections, which we refer to as residual plasticity.

As additional representational capacity can hinder generalisation, especially in RL [25,26,27], we propose a joint-rational variant that uses weight-sharing in rational activations across different layers.

We empirically demonstrate that rational activations bring significant improvements to DQN and Rainbow algorithms on Atari games, and that our joint variant further increases performance.

Finally, we investigate the overestimation phenomenon of predicting too large return values, previously argued to originate from an unsuitable representational capacity of the learning architecture [28]. As a result of our introduced (rational) neural and residual plasticity, such overestimation can be practically reduced.

We proceed as follows. We start by arguing in favour of plasticity for deep RL, then show how rational functions are particularly suitable candidates for providing plasticity in neural networks, and present our empirical evaluation. Before concluding, we touch upon related work.
